Exercise 7.1 · Week 7

Save High Scores

Python in Thonny Work in pairs

Goal: make Lucky Dice remember every score, even after the program closes.

Right now the program forgets everything when it stops. You will save each game as one line in a text file called high_scores.txt:

Ada,120
Kai,95
  1. Open starter.py in Thonny and press Run. Play twice. Does it remember your first game? (Not yet!)
  2. TODO 1 save_score(): open the file with "a" (append = add to the end) and write one line nickname,score.
  3. TODO 2 load_scores(): for every line, strip() it, skip empty lines, split(",") it and add [nickname, score] to the list. The score must be a number: int(parts[1]).
  4. TODO 3 the file might not exist yet (first game ever). Make an empty one with "w".
  5. Run the game three times. Then open high_scores.txt in Thonny (File > Open, same folder) and look at your saved scores.

Done looks like: "Games saved so far" goes up by one every time you play, and the high score is the best one from all the games.

Careful: "w" wipes the file clean before writing. Use "a" to add.

Extra: print every saved game as a numbered list (1. Ada - 120), or show how many games each nickname has played (a dictionary is perfect).

Privacy: save nicknames and scores only. Never save real names, ages or where you live.

Starter code

Open starter.py in Thonny, or copy the code below into a new file and save it as starter.py.

# Save High Scores
# Right now the program FORGETS every score when it closes.
# Your job: save each score in a file, and read the file back.
# Each line of the file holds one game:   nickname,score
# Do the TODOs in order. Press Run after each one.

import random

SCORE_FILE = "high_scores.txt"


def save_score(filename, nickname, score):
    """Add one line 'nickname,score' to the end of the file."""
    # TODO 1: open the file in "a" (append) mode and write ONE line.
    # Hint:
    #     with open(filename, "a") as file:
    #         file.write(f"{nickname},{score}\n")
    pass


def load_scores(filename):
    """Return a list of [nickname, score] pairs, one for each line.
    If the file is missing, make an empty one and return []."""
    scores = []
    try:
        with open(filename, "r") as file:
            for line in file:
                # TODO 2: 1) line = line.strip()
                #         2) if the line is not empty (""):
                #         3)     parts = line.split(",")
                #         4)     append [parts[0], int(parts[1])] to scores
                pass
    except FileNotFoundError:
        # TODO 3: the file is missing. Make an empty one by opening it
        # in "w" (write) mode and writing "" (nothing).
        pass
    return scores


def best_score(scores):
    """Return the [nickname, score] pair with the highest score.
    An empty list gives ["nobody yet", 0]."""
    best = ["nobody yet", 0]
    for entry in scores:
        if entry[1] > best[1]:
            best = entry
    return best


def roll_three_dice():
    """Roll three dice, print each roll, and return the total times 10."""
    total = 0
    for roll in range(3):
        die = random.randint(1, 6)
        print(f"Roll {roll + 1}: {die}")
        total = total + die
    return total * 10


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Lucky Dice: roll three dice and beat the high score! ===")
    nickname = input("Your nickname (not your real name): ")
    score = roll_three_dice()
    print(f"{nickname}, you scored {score}!")

    save_score(SCORE_FILE, nickname, score)
    scores = load_scores(SCORE_FILE)
    best = best_score(scores)
    print(f"Games saved so far: {len(scores)}")
    print(f"High score: {best[0]} with {best[1]}")

Stuck? Open a hint

Try on your own first. Hints open one at a time, from a small nudge to a bigger one. None of them gives the answer away.

Hint 1: Where to look

Look at the top of starter.py for the three TODOs. save_score() is the first one. It has to put a line in the file so the game can remember it next time.

Hint 2: Try this

open(filename, "a") opens a file so new text is added at the end. file.write(...) puts text in it. For reading, line.strip() removes the hidden newline, and split(",") cuts a line into pieces.

Hint 3: Almost there

Use with open(filename, "____") as file: then file.write(f"{____},{____}\n"). When reading, turn the second piece into a number with int(parts[____]). Missing file? Open it with "____" and write nothing.
